title: Highest-Protein Nuts: Ranking Per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Nuts Ranked per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare almonds, pistachios, cashews, walnuts and other nuts by protein per 100 grams and per one-ounce serving.

excerpt: Almonds and pistachios lead common tree nuts at roughly 20–21 grams of protein per 100 grams. A realistic one-ounce serving, however, contributes closer to 5–6 grams.
content_html:
Nuts are protein-containing foods, but most of their calories come from fat. That makes them impressive per 100 grams and much less extreme when viewed per serving or per calorie.

Protein ranking

NutProtein/100 gProtein/1 oz (28 g)
Almondsabout 21 gabout 6 g
Pistachiosabout 20 g5.5–6 g
Cashewsabout 18 gabout 5 g
Walnutsabout 15 gabout 4 g
Hazelnutsabout 15 gabout 4 g
Brazil nutsabout 14 gabout 4 g
Pecansabout 9 g2.5 g
Macadamiasabout 8 g2 g

Where are peanuts?

Peanuts would win at roughly 25–26 g per 100 g, but botanically they are legumes rather than tree nuts. They are nutritionally and culinarily similar enough to mention, but separating them keeps the ranking technically clear.

Almonds and pistachios

Both provide around six grams per ounce, along with fiber, unsaturated fats and minerals. They are useful additions to breakfast, snacks or salads, but an ounce does not replace the protein in a full serving of beans, tofu, fish or poultry.

Walnuts trade some protein for a different fat profile

Walnuts contain less protein but stand out for alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), a plant omega-3. A protein-only ranking therefore undersells them.

Raw versus roasted

Roasting changes moisture and can slightly shift per-weight numbers. It does not remove protein. Commercial coatings, frying oils, sugar and sodium usually matter more than the raw-versus-roasted distinction.

Protein per calorie: why nuts are not a lean protein source

The ranking looks impressive by weight, but nuts are energy-dense. One ounce of almonds provides roughly 6 g of protein and about 160–165 calories; an ounce of pistachios provides about 6 g and roughly 160 calories. For comparison, 100 g of cooked chicken breast is in a similar calorie range—around 165 calories—but provides about 31 g of protein. That does not make almonds or pistachios inferior foods; it shows that their nutritional role is different.

Nuts combine protein with unsaturated fat, fiber and micronutrients. They are excellent for adding a few grams of protein to breakfast, snacks or salads, but they are much less efficient if the only goal is maximizing protein for a fixed calorie budget.

Which nut makes the most sense in a normal serving?

The top of the table is close. A one-ounce serving of almonds gives about 6 g of protein, pistachios about 5.5–6 g and cashews about 5 g. Choosing almonds over pistachios for a difference of a few tenths of a gram is unlikely to matter in practice.

Other nutrients can be a better tie-breaker. Walnuts provide ALA omega-3; almonds are notable for vitamin E; pistachios contribute potassium and vitamin B6; cashews provide copper, magnesium and zinc. A varied mix often makes more nutritional sense than repeatedly buying whichever nut sits first in a protein ranking.

What about nut butters?

Grinding a nut into butter does not remove its protein, but serving size changes how easy it is to eat a large amount. Two tablespoons of almond butter typically provide around 6–7 g of protein and roughly 190–200 calories, depending on the product. Added sugar, oils and salt can also change the label.

If protein is the reason for buying a nut butter, compare products per two-tablespoon serving rather than assuming all jars are equivalent. A short ingredient list also makes it easier to understand what you are actually comparing.

Brazil nuts are a special case

Brazil nuts are not especially high in protein compared with almonds or pistachios, but they are extremely rich in selenium. That means eating large quantities simply to chase more protein is a poor trade-off. Their value comes from a distinctive micronutrient profile, not from winning the protein table.

Bottom line

Among common tree nuts, almonds and pistachios are the strongest protein options at roughly 20–21 g per 100 g, or about 6 g per ounce. Cashews follow at around 18 g per 100 g. The practical difference between the leaders is small, so portion size, calories and the rest of the nutrient profile matter more than the exact podium.

Frequently asked questions

Which nut has the most protein?

Among common tree nuts, almonds and pistachios lead at about 20–21 g per 100 g.

Are peanuts higher?

Yes, but peanuts are legumes botanically.

How much protein is in an ounce of nuts?

Roughly 2–6 g depending on the nut, with almonds and pistachios near the upper end.

faq.question: Which nut is highest in protein?
faq.answer: Almonds and pistachios are among the highest common tree nuts at about 20–21 g per 100 g.

faq.question: Why are peanuts excluded?
faq.answer: They are botanically legumes, even though they are used like nuts.

faq.question: How much protein does a one-ounce serving provide?
faq.answer: Usually about 2–6 g depending on the nut.
